lines.text:
Shopping at the Market

Every Saturday morning, I go to the outdoor market in the town centre. It is much bigger than a supermarket, and I enjoy the atmosphere — the colours, the smells, and the sound of vendors calling out their prices.

The fruit and vegetable stalls are always the busiest. Fresh apples, oranges, bananas, and berries are arranged in neat rows. The vegetables — tomatoes, potatoes, onions, peppers, and lettuce — are weighed on a scale, and you pay by the kilogram.

Next to the produce section, there is a butcher's stall with different cuts of meat: chicken, lamb, and beef. Across from it, the fishmonger sells fresh fish, shrimp, and squid laid out on ice. The cheese stall offers dozens of varieties, and you can taste samples before buying.

There is also a bakery stall with fresh bread, pastries, and cakes. The smell of warm bread fills the air every morning. Nearby, a spice vendor sells bags of cumin, turmeric, cinnamon, and dried herbs.

I always bring my shopping bag and a list. I compare prices between stalls before choosing. Some vendors give you a discount if you buy in bulk. At the end of the morning, when the market is about to close, you can sometimes get a bargain.

I pay with cash at most stalls, but some now accept card payments. The market is not only a place to shop — it is a social experience where neighbours meet, chat, and share recipes.

lines.text: In English-speaking countries, 'market' usually means an outdoor or covered market with individual stalls. A 'supermarket' is a large self-service shop. 'Farmers' market' sells directly from producers.
lines.name: In English-speaking countries, 'market' usually means an outdoor or covered market with individual stalls. A 'supermarket' is a large self-service shop. 'Farmers' market' sells directly from producers.

lines.text: British: 'stall' / American: 'stand' or 'booth'. British: 'queue' / American: 'line'. British: 'till' / American: 'register' or 'checkout'. British: 'shop' / American: 'store'.
lines.name: British: 'stall' / American: 'stand' or 'booth'. British: 'queue' / American: 'line'. British: 'till' / American: 'register' or 'checkout'. British: 'shop' / American: 'store'.

lines.text: Haggling (negotiating the price) is common at markets in many countries but rare in UK/US shops and supermarkets. At car boot sales or flea markets, gentle bargaining is acceptable.
lines.name: Haggling (negotiating the price) is common at markets in many countries but rare in UK/US shops and supermarkets. At car boot sales or flea markets, gentle bargaining is acceptable.

lines.text: UK markets use both kilograms and pounds (weight). US markets use pounds and ounces. Understanding 'a pound of apples' (≈450g) vs 'a kilo of apples' is useful.
lines.name: UK markets use both kilograms and pounds (weight). US markets use pounds and ounces. Understanding 'a pound of apples' (≈450g) vs 'a kilo of apples' is useful.

lines.text: 'Organic' = grown without synthetic chemicals. 'Free-range' = animals allowed to roam outdoors. 'Fair trade' = producers in developing countries receive a fair price. These labels are common at English markets.
